title: What's Next for Nvidia?
author: zdw
relevanceReason: 命中 8 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: Nvidia’s board announced that Jensen Huang had resigned 33 years after he co-founded the company. What happens to a company when a visionary CEO is gone? Most often innovation dies and the company coasts for years on momentum and its brand. Rarely does it regain its former glory. That’s the danger facing Nvidia. Here’s what their board should be considering. Here’s why.

Jensen Huang reinvented Nvidia three times. In 2006 he launched CUDA, turning a graphics chip for PC gamers into a general-purpose computing platform – and funded it for years ahead of any revenue. In 2012, when researchers used Nvidia chips to win the ImageNet contest, he pointed the company to deep learning. In 2020, with the acquisition of Mellanox, Nvidia went from selling boards with GPUs to selling integrated racks that power AI datacenters. These were not just product transitions, but radical business model transitions; new channels, new customers and new markets. Nvidia pivoted from a vendor of graphics boards, to a software platform, and then to systems company. It’s hard to imagine a CEO focused on executing an existing business model funding CUDA through those years.

Steve Jobs did the same at Apple, transforming it from a niche computer company into the most profitable company in the world. Between 2001 and 2008, Jobs reinvented the company three times. Visionary CEOs are not “just” great at assuring world-class execution of a successful business model, they are also world-class innovators. The best are agile and know how to pivot, making substantive changes to their business model while or before their market has shifted. The very best of them shape markets – they know how to create new markets by seeing opportunities before anyone else. They remain entrepreneurs.

Visionary CEOs don’t need someone else to demo the company’s key products for them. They deeply understand products, and they have their own coherent and consistent vision of where the industry/business models and customers are today, and where they need to take the company. They know who their customers are because they spend time talking to them. They use strategy committees and the exec staff for advice, but none of these CEOs pivot by committee. Microsoft and Apple are two examples of what happens when a visionary CEO is replaced by an execution CEO. Microsoft and the Cost of Missing the Next Market Microsoft entered the 21st century as the dominant software provider for anyone who interacted with a computing device. After running Microsoft for 25 years, Bill Gates handed the reins of Microsoft to Steve Ballmer in January 2000. Ballmer went on to run Microsoft for the next 14 years. Ballmer organized the company around execution of its then current strengths – Windows and Office businesses. He tripled Microsoft’s sales to $78 billion and profits more than doubled from $9 billion to $22 billion, but those results hid missed opportunities that would reshape computing. Ballmer failed to understand and execute on the five most important technology trends of the 21st century: in search – losing to Google; in smartphones – losing to Apple; in mobile operating systems – losing to Google/Apple; in media – losing to Apple/Netflix; and in the cloud – losing to Amazon. In early 2014, Satya Nadella took charge. Nadella got Microsoft organized around the cloud (Azure), freed the Office and Azure teams from Windows and killed the phone business. Nadella saved Microsoft from irrelevance. Today Microsoft is worth about $4 trillion. It is one of the few companies that regained its former glory, after its board replaced a salesman with a product and engineering insider. Innovation CEOs Hire Execution VPs Successful visionary CEOs build an executive staff of world-class operating executives and technical leaders (and they unconsciously force out any world-class innovators from their direct reports). The problem is in a company driven by a visionary CEO; there is only one visionary.

Nvidia is the extreme case. Jensen had about 60 direct reports and discouraged one-on-one meetings. No long-term plans. Much like Jobs, he made himself the point where technical, product and business decisions came together. Replacing that role is harder than filling a box on an organization chart. He said he didn’t believe in succession planning.

comments.author: areoform
comments.textRawHtml:
What made Steve Jobs great was that he would rather have Apple cannibalize its successful product lines than fall prey to a competitor. You can see this pattern with the iPod. The iPod disrupted itself many, many times. The iPod Mini then the iPod Nano. Then the iPod shuffle as the answer to the race ot the bottom.

The biggest moment was partnering with Motorola as phones started becoming more capable and flash memory got cheaper to bring music to phones, which was then the prelude to the iPhone.

The iPhone killed the iPod. Most companies would have never created the product, because it would have killed their golden goose, but Jobs did.

Just like he went all in on the iPad which had the potential to kill the cheap student Mac.

If Nvidia's next CEO is smart, they'd buy up a bunch of these companies that "burn" weights to silicon, make the process better, and then sell that as a service. Let it cannibalize the sales of their products. It's better for them to do it to themselves than their competitors.

children.author: CoolestBeans
children.textRawHtml:
Jensen's strategy has been to stimulate demand and then own as big a chunk of it as you can. This is the strategy of GPGPUs and CUDA. Have developers go create new demand for your cards and then lock them in. And they did. Financially, the circular deals are similar. Getting into making ASIC inference chips, you don't own the demand and you're making a commodity so you can't lock people in.

Steve Jobs was completely unsentimental about obsoleting Apple's lineup with new products but that's because Steve Jobs's strategy was to be a ruthless fast follower. Just wait for the technology to catch up with a burgeoning product category and then come out with a product with way more polish and sensible UX than everyone else. That's great for consumer electronics but its not so great for Nvidia. There's a lot less value in "taste" and "polish" when it comes to a device that's going to sit in a data center for its whole life.

children.author: torginus
children.textRawHtml:
I am surprised nobody caught up to CUDA. Back in the early 10s I wrote my thesis in OpenCL, and I picked it on a whim, tooling seemed about equal.

Since then, OpenCL fell off completely while the CUDA of today doesn't seem all that different to my cursory inspection. Also, I'm not sure how high-level a language modern CUDA is, considering that back then it was common wisdom that every uArch was so different that you could easily lose more than half of the performance if you didn't optimize for it, which often meant swapping out entire algorithms or changing how the data is laid out. This applied to moving between vendors and moving to newer generations from the same vendor. So programming CUDA was much more about trying to coax the compiler into generating the right sort of assembly.

Besides, my impression is that the kernels that run LLMs are a relatively small-ish (thousands of lines). Even with awful tooling, you can get a couple engineers to port the code to your architecture of choice, or nowadays, you can get the agents themselves to do it for you.

children.textRawHtml:
I think CUDA has the same advantage that Apple has: It's entirely in-house, and engineers only need to optimise for in-house hardware. That means that design decisions can be made that only make sense for NVIDIA hardware, rather than (with OpenCL) providing an API that can be implemented by a much broader range of hardware. That narrower focus means that a) the API can move more quickly as new GPU features are made available (did you know that OpenCL still doesn't have support for bindless images!?), and b) as the surface is smaller and more hardware-specific, it can be optimised and tuned more effectively.

The other answer is that NVIDIA's offering isn't really CUDA - it's the various libraries like cuBLAS, cuDNN, CUTLASS, etc that provide extremely high performance kernels for machine learning and other gpu-relevant tasks. That's where NVIDIA locks in customers, as producing such high-quality libraries is extremely hard (many of the kernels for cuBLAS are written in uarchitecture-specific asm), and they get to define the interface, which means that it's hard for engineers to write portable code.

children.author: sandworm101
children.textRawHtml: I think the CUDA lock-in is a bit of a sham. As said, it can be ported to another architecture. A competitor could/will show up eventually. The real lock-in imho is the memory shortage. Nvidia has a grip over the chip contracts. Even if someone appeared today with a non-nvidia card that could run any CUDA job perfectly, that competitor couldn't get those cards built.

children.author: Betelbuddy
children.textRawHtml:
If you look at the history of NVIDIA, they made terrible mistakes and were at the verge of bankruptcy at multiple critical times in their history. Jensen Huang mentioned this several times in more that one interview.

They could have been a niche gaming company, and four years ago their stock price was...$12 ...yeah 12 dollars, that is a bubble for you, and can go back to $12 as quickly.

He got hit on the head with AI....And essentially, got the lottery ticket of the mechanical sympathy of GPUs, having the ideal architecture for the core algorithm of a technological revolution, that only happens every 50 years.

A computer science advance can as well quickly, make their GPUs obsolete. The Jev model being a possible example, even if yes, you still need the GPUs for Training.

It was not long that for their talk of AI, they were hanging up the phone on Geoffrey Hinton, when he was begging for a donation of one GPU: https://youtu.be/n4IQOBka8bc?t=1352

You need the merit to be at right place and right time, but the analysis of what NVIDIA needs seems to forget the most important: The need their luck not to turn...

If you know CUDA in depth, you will know there is not much there, its not a deep layer, and I am surprised ZLUDA or SCALE are not taking more adoption.

children.author: embedding-shape
children.textRawHtml:
> It was not long that for their talk of AI, they were hanging up the phone on Geoffrey Hinton, when he was begging for a donation of one GPU: https://youtu.be/n4IQOBka8bc?t=1352

That's a bit of a misquote. He told N machine learning people to get a nvidia GPU, then after that he sent an email telling (someone at) nvidia he had done that and asked for a free GPU, no one replied, later met Jensen, who gave him a free GPU. Might have been he sent an email to corporate@nvidia.com or whatever, who knows?

> If you know CUDA in depth, you will know there is not much there, its not a deep layer, and I am surprised ZLUDA or SCALE are not taking more adoption.

If you're using CUDA in depth in practice, you know that there is so much more to it than just the APIs CUDA specifically offer, as those are as you say not so deep. All the debugging, profiling and introspection tools also comes with it, just to scratch the surface of what you get for "free" once you start leaning on CUDA.

Six months after the release, AMD legal department ordered Janik to delete the AMD funded codebase from GitHub. AMD claimed that the earlier email permission he received to open-source the project was "not legally binding" - https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/gpu-drivers/cuda-...

Maybe with REA (Reverse Engineer Anything), the solution will come as everybody building their own CUDA?
